scenario_prompt: Write the risk section of a solution proposal, naming each material risk and what is done about it, and stating plainly any risk that cannot be fully retired rather than omitting it. Context: the buyer's RFP requires a SOC 2 Type II report and the bidder holds only a SOC 2 Type I report today, with the Type II observation window closing after the RFP's submission date; separately, the bidder's own most comparable prior migration took 11 months, close to the buyer's 6-month compliance-audit deadline. Return only the risk section text.
text:
## 7. Risks and Mitigations

We have set out below every material risk we currently see in this engagement, including the two that we cannot fully retire before award. We would rather name them here than have them surface during contracting.

**7.1 Certification gap: we hold SOC 2 Type I, not Type II (cannot be fully retired before submission)**

The RFP requires a SOC 2 Type II report. We hold a SOC 2 Type I report covering the in-scope systems. Our Type II observation window is currently open and closes after this RFP's submission date, which means we cannot produce a Type II report by the date the buyer has asked for one. This is a real gap against a stated requirement, not a documentation delay.

What we are doing: our Type I attestation covers the same control set and the same system boundary that the Type II will cover, so the control design the buyer is evaluating is already independently examined. We will provide the Type I report, the auditor's engagement letter confirming the Type II observation period and its close date, and a bridge letter from our auditor. We will accept a contractual commitment to deliver the Type II report within [X] days of its issuance, with a defined remedy if we fail to do so.

What remains: until the report issues, the buyer is accepting a Type I where it specified Type II. If the auditor identifies exceptions during the observation window, the resulting report could contain qualifications we cannot predict today. No mitigation we can offer changes that, and the buyer should weigh it as a genuine open item rather than a formality.

**7.2 Schedule risk against the 6-month compliance-audit deadline (cannot be fully retired)**

The buyer's compliance audit falls 6 months after start. Our most comparable prior migration took 11 months. We are not going to present 6 months as a comfortable target; on our own track record it is aggressive.

What we are doing: we have decomposed the programme so that the systems in the audit's scope are migrated and evidence-producing first, with non-audit-scope workloads deliberately sequenced after the deadline. The 11-month prior engagement carried roughly [X] months of discovery and data-quality remediation that we have since productised, and it ran without a dedicated cutover team; this bid staffs one. We propose a go/no-go checkpoint at month 3 with agreed scope-reduction options defined in advance, so that a slip is detected and acted on while there is still room to act.

What remains: our own most relevant data point is 11 months, and re-planning does not by itself make the work smaller. If discovery reveals data conditions materially worse than in the environments we have assessed, the audit-scope subset may still not complete in 6 months. The realistic protection is not certainty of delivery but early warning and a pre-agreed fallback, and we recommend the buyer identify now what a defensible partial position at the audit looks like.

**7.3 Data quality and undocumented dependencies in the source estate**

Prior migrations of this type consistently surface undocumented integrations and records that fail validation. Mitigation: a structured discovery phase in weeks 1–4 with automated dependency scanning and a reconciliation harness that runs continuously rather than at cutover. Residual risk is moderate and is the most likely single cause of the schedule risk in 7.2 materialising.

**7.4 Key-person dependency**

The named leads in Section 5 carry material engagement-specific knowledge. Mitigation: each named role has an identified deputy engaged from week 1, and we commit contractually to notice and equivalent-seniority replacement. Residual risk is low but not zero.

**7.5 Buyer-side resource availability**

The plan assumes the buyer's SMEs are available at the levels set out in Section 6. Shortfalls here directly consume the limited schedule float described in 7.2. Mitigation: availability is stated as a dependency in the contract with a defined change-control trigger, so any shortfall is visible and costed rather than silently absorbed.
